text:
Here are three distributions, each drawn on its own axis. They look alike. And mixing them up is how confidence intervals get misread. So let's pull them apart.

The first is the population. Here, that's what a million customers spend. They spend fifty dollars on average, with a spread of eighteen. It's wide, it's fixed... and in real life, you almost never get to see it. The second is one sample. Pick forty customers at random. It's a noisy snapshot of the population. Ragged, but about as wide, with a spread of about twenty. That's what a histogram of your data shows. Raw values, one per customer.

The third is a different kind of thing. Average those forty, and you get one number... about forty-seven dollars. That average becomes one block in a new chart. Now pick forty more, and forty more. Five thousand samples later, the averages have piled up right on fifty. And their spread is under three dollars.

On their own axes, these three looked alike. On one axis, the widths tell them apart. The population and the sample are raw values, spread across tens of dollars. The third is a statistic, one average per sample. And it barely moves. That gap is why forty customers can pin down the average of a million. And a histogram of your data? It's always the middle one.

Now, here's a trap. A simulation has two ways to get more data... more samples, or bigger ones. Draw more samples, from five hundred up to thirty-two thousand, and the histogram just gets smoother. Its spread stays near two point eight. Make each sample bigger, from ten customers up to six hundred and forty, and the spread falls, from five and a half to under one. And in real life, you only ever get ONE sample. Its size is the lever you actually control.

One last thing. The mean isn't special. Every statistic has a sampling distribution. Take samples of sixty from a lopsided population, like incomes, and keep each sample's mean, median and maximum. Each gets its own center, its own width, and its own shape. The maximum lands far out, wide and lopsided. And that width, how far a statistic moves from one sample to the next, has a name... the standard error.
